meta.title: Who really said "Things may come to those who wait, but only the things left by those who hustle"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Lincoln. It first appears as a newspaper filler in May 1955 — ninety years after he died — and the earliest located Lincoln credit is 1972, in an Australian newspaper. It is absent from Basler's Collected Works.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Things may come to those who wait, but only the things left by those who hustle'?
meta.ogDescription: A 1955 newspaper one-liner of unknown authorship. Lincoln died in 1865; the credit was bolted on in the 1970s.

answer.label: Not Abraham Lincoln — an anonymous newspaper filler from 1955
answer.sourceLine: Lincoln died in 1865. The saying first appears in May 1955, as an unattributed one-liner in American local newspapers — the short filler items editors used to plug a column. The earliest located instance credited to Lincoln is from 27 January 1972, in The Age of Melbourne, where a firm quoted it as its motto. It appears nowhere in the Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, which is fully searchable, and the Abraham Lincoln Association rejected it in 2003.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Things may come to those who wait, but only the things that are left by those who hustle.
trail: The earliest instances located by the quotation researcher Barry Popik are both from the same week of May 1955: the Times Herald of Carroll, Iowa on 9 May, and the Anderson, Indiana Daily Bulletin on 10 May, in a column of one-line jokes called ‘Barbs.’ Neither carries an author. That syndicated-filler pattern is the signature of an anonymous gag, not a presidential aphorism the citations ↗.

The Lincoln credit is much later. The earliest documented instance is 27 January 1972, in The Age (Melbourne, Australia) — a company using the line as a corporate motto and crediting Lincoln for it. Seventeen years of anonymous circulation come first.

Lincoln’s writings are exceptionally well mapped: Roy P. Basler’s nine-volume Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln is complete, indexed and searchable online. The saying is not in it, in any wording. Absence from a searchable corpus is not proof of a negative in general — but for Lincoln it comes close, which is why the Abraham Lincoln Association put this line on its rejected list in 2003.

There is an older cousin worth knowing: ‘All things come to him who hustles while he waits’ is in print by 1893 and is itself commonly misattributed — usually to Thomas Edison. The 1955 line is a sharper rewrite of that Gilded-Age joke, not an inheritance from the 1860s.
source.excerptNote: The earliest located wording. Note the extra words — ‘the things that are left’ — which the version people quote has trimmed. Sayings get shorter as they travel; that shortening is one of the ways you can tell circulation has been at work on a line.
source.rightsNote: We give no rights status. The 1955 newspaper appearances are anonymous filler items with no identifiable author, and while unrenewed US periodical content of that period is very often in the public domain, that depends on facts about renewal we have not checked for these specific papers. What is clear is that the Lincoln route to public domain does not apply — he did not write it, so his 1865 death date is irrelevant here. Quote it as an anonymous 1950s saying. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Abraham Lincoln
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Lincoln
author.bio: Abraham Lincoln led the United States through the Civil War and was assassinated in April 1865. He is American English’s favourite unpaid endorser: rail-splitter to president, self-taught, famously hard-working, and dead long enough that nobody expects a footnote. Any homespun line about effort beating luck will drift to him eventually. There is an extra irony here — in Lincoln’s own lifetime ‘hustle’ mostly meant to shove or to hurry, not the 20th-century sense of grinding ambition the saying depends on. The word gives the game away before the archives do.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is one of the easier ones to settle, because Lincoln is the best-documented American of the 19th century and the saying is a piece of mid-century newspaper furniture with a date on it.

items.why: The line first appears in 1955; Lincoln died in 1865. It is absent from Basler’s Collected Works, which is complete and searchable, and the Abraham Lincoln Association placed it on its rejected list in 2003. There is no speech, letter, fragment or reported remark the citations ↗.

The earliest located Lincoln attribution is The Age (Melbourne), 27 January 1972 — a business quoting it as its motto. That is unusually satisfying: we can watch a saying circulate anonymously for seventeen years, get adopted as a corporate slogan, and acquire a president in the same sentence.

items.who: ‘All things come to him who hustles while he waits’
items.why: In print by 1893 and usually credited to Thomas Edison, on no evidence. The 1955 saying is a rewrite of it, which places both firmly in the industrial-optimism tradition rather than anywhere near Lincoln.

items.who: ‘Good things come to those who wait’
items.why: The straight proverb is much older and is usually traced to a 19th-century poem by Violet Fane. The Lincoln line is a joke at its expense — which is why the two are constantly mashed into ‘Good things come to those who wait, but only what’s left…’ That hybrid has no source either.

The saying needs 'hustle' to mean relentless self-advancing effort. That sense is a late-19th and 20th-century American development; in Lincoln's day the word leaned much more towards shoving and hurrying. The sentence could not have carried its punchline in 1860.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous American newspaper one-liner, first located on 9 May 1955, which acquired Lincoln’s name in the early 1970s. He has no connection to it, and his complete works are searchable if you want to check the Collected Works ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is a joke with a grievance in it. The old proverb tells you to be patient; this one points out that patience is a strategy with a queue in front of it, and that the people at the front are not waiting. Anyone who has watched a promotion go to the person who asked for it recognises the sentiment instantly.

It also explains its own attribution. A line about the rewards of hustle wants a self-made hero, and American English has one on permanent standby. Bolting it to Lincoln converts a wisecrack from a 1955 filler column into national wisdom — which is a fairly hustling thing to do to a quotation about hustling.
detailsBody: 1865: Lincoln is assassinated. Nothing resembling this line exists in his papers.
1893: 'All things come to him who hustles while he waits' is in print — anonymous, later misattributed to Edison.
9 May 1955: earliest located instance of this saying, Times Herald, Carroll, Iowa — unattributed.
10 May 1955: the Anderson, Indiana Daily Bulletin runs it in its 'Barbs' column of one-liners.
27 January 1972: earliest located Lincoln credit, The Age, Melbourne — quoted as a company motto.
2003: the Abraham Lincoln Association lists it among things Lincoln did not say.
context.pull: Seventeen years anonymous, then a corporate motto, then a president. In that order.
